lede: Human insulin can be made by bacteria that carry a human gene. It takes an enzyme that cuts DNA at one sequence, a small ring of bacterial DNA to carry the gene, and a tank of multiplying bacteria. Every stage has one name the exam asks for, and one stage asks you to count.
can: Describe the stages of making human insulin in order, with the name for each one.
Find where a restriction enzyme cuts a base sequence, and count the sections it leaves.
Explain why one enzyme cuts both the gene and the plasmid, and what downstreaming is for.

md: Someone with type 1 diabetes injects insulin, and it can be human insulin made by bacteria. Getting a bacterium to make a human protein takes one gene, two cuts, one join and a very large tank.

alt: Six stages: a restriction enzyme cuts the insulin gene out of human DNA; the same enzyme opens a plasmid; the gene is joined into it; the plasmid goes into a bacterium; the bacteria multiply in a fermenter; the insulin is extracted, purified and packaged.

md:
An organism's **genome** is all of its genetic material. **Genetic engineering** changes the genome to give the organism a **desirable characteristic**. A **gene** is a section of DNA coding for one protein, and insulin is a protein.

In the figure, the bacterium's genome is its chromosome plus its plasmid. Join the human insulin gene into the plasmid and the genome has changed: that is the engineering. The characteristic gained: making human insulin.

prompt: What is the genome of an organism?
options: all of its genetic material
one of its genes
the protein one gene codes for
explain: The genome means the whole of an organism's genetic material: every gene on every chromosome, and in a bacterium the plasmid too. A gene is one section of it, and a protein is what a gene codes for. So the genome is all of its genetic material.

text: 2. Why a bacterium makes a human protein

md: Every living thing writes its genes in the same four bases, and a gene is the code for one protein. Insulin is a protein, so the insulin gene carries everything needed to make it. A bacterium reads whatever gene it holds and joins **amino acids** in the order that gene sets.

Follow the figure downwards: the gene, read by the bacterium, becomes a chain of amino acids in the gene's order, and that chain is insulin. Why a plasmid? A bacterium copies its plasmids every time it divides, so a gene joined into one is copied too: one bacterium becomes billions, all making insulin.

prompt: A bacterium carries the human insulin gene in its plasmid. Why does it make human insulin?
options: it reads the gene and builds the protein from amino acids
the gene turns into insulin inside the plasmid
the plasmid holds a store of insulin
answer: it reads the gene and builds the protein from amino acids
explain: A gene is a code for one protein, and a bacterium reads any gene it carries, joining amino acids in the order the gene sets. The plasmid holds the code, never the hormone: no insulin exists until the bacterium builds it. So it reads the gene and builds the protein from amino acids.

md: A **restriction enzyme** cuts DNA only where it finds one particular **base sequence**. Each enzyme has its own, and a question always says which. This lesson's enzyme looks for TCGA.

**Cut the top strand** between T and C, reading left to right.
**Cut the bottom strand** between its own T and C, reading right to left: two bases further along.
**The result:** a staggered cut, with a few unpaired bases on each piece: **sticky ends**.

title: Why the ends are sticky
md: The unpaired bases on one end are complementary to those on the other: C pairs with G, G with C. Any two ends this enzyme leaves can pair up again, like the halves of a zip.

prompt: The short single-stranded ends left by a restriction enzyme's staggered cut are called ______ ends.
explain: The staggered cut leaves a few unpaired bases on each piece, and because those bases are complementary the pieces can pair up again: that is what makes the ends sticky. Loose or matching describes them, but the name the mark scheme wants is sticky ends.

md: The paper prints a length of DNA, tells you the enzyme's sequence, and asks you to mark every cut and count the sections. Three steps, every time; here they are on the figure.

**Step 1: find every site.** Read the top strand from the left: TCGA at bases 3 to 6 and 11 to 14.
**Step 2: one site, one staggered cut.** The bottom strand under each site reads TCGA from right to left, so it is cut too, two bases along: 2 cuts.
**Step 3: count the sections.** A straight length already has two ends, so every cut adds one section: 2 + 1 = **3 sections**.

prompt: The same enzyme cuts between T and C wherever the top strand reads TCGA. This top strand reads ACTCGATTGTCGACTTCGAG. Into how many sections is this length of DNA cut?
explain: Step 1, find every TCGA on the top strand: bases 3 to 6, 10 to 13 and 16 to 19. Step 2, one site is one staggered cut, so 3 cuts. Step 3, a straight length already has two ends, so sections are cuts plus one: 3 + 1 = 4 sections.

md:
Count ends, not pieces. A straight length starts with 2 ends. Every cut makes 2 new ends, so after n cuts there are 2 + 2n ends. Each section has 2 ends, so the number of sections is (2 + 2n) ÷ 2 = n + 1.

A ring starts with no ends. After n cuts it has 2n ends, so n pieces: the first cut only opens it.
Check it on the figure. The straight piece, 3 cuts: 2 + 6 = 8 ends, so 8 ÷ 2 = 4 sections. The ring, 3 cuts: 6 ends, so 3 pieces.

prompt: A circular plasmid is cut in 5 places by a restriction enzyme. How many pieces are produced?
explain: A ring has no ends to begin with, so its first cut only opens it and each cut after that adds one piece: n cuts give n pieces. 5 cuts make 10 ends, and 10 ÷ 2 = 5 pieces. On a straight length it would be 5 + 1 = 6.

md: A **plasmid** is a small ring of DNA in a bacterium, separate from its chromosome. The **same restriction enzyme** cuts it open. It cuts at the same base sequence, so the plasmid's sticky ends are **complementary** to the gene's.

**Step 1.** Cut the plasmid open with the same enzyme: on a ring, one cut opens it without making pieces.
**Step 2.** The gene's sticky ends pair with the plasmid's, so the gene sits in the gap.
**Step 3.** The gene is joined in. The ring is now a **modified plasmid**, also called a recombinant plasmid.

prompt: Why is the plasmid cut with the same restriction enzyme that cut out the insulin gene?
options: so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join
so the enzyme is used up
so the plasmid falls into many pieces
answer: so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join
explain: A restriction enzyme cuts at one base sequence every time, so the ends it leaves on the plasmid match the ends it left on the gene, and complementary ends pair up. A different enzyme would leave ends that do not pair. So the same enzyme is used so that the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join.

md: The modified plasmid is put into a bacterium, which is now **genetically modified**. The modified bacteria are grown in a **fermenter**: a large stirred vessel, kept warm and fed. Three things happen inside it:

1. The bacteria **multiply**.
2. Their plasmids are **copied** each time, so every new bacterium has the gene.
3. The bacteria make their proteins, and one of them is **human insulin**: a protein built from **amino acids** in the order the gene codes for.

title: The gene, not the hormone
md: Summer 2024's report names this: answers saying the plasmid contained the hormone could not score. The plasmid carries the **insulin gene**. The insulin does not exist until the bacterium makes it.

prompt: In the fermenter, what happens to the genetically modified bacteria and their plasmids?
options: they multiply
they are purified
they are cut open
explain: The fermenter's job is numbers: a few modified bacteria become billions, and their plasmids are copied with them, so every new bacterium carries the gene. The cutting happened before the plasmid went in, and purifying happens after, in downstreaming. So in the fermenter they multiply.

md: At the end the fermenter holds a broth of bacteria, leftover food, waste and insulin. **Downstreaming** turns it into a medicine in three stages: **extraction** (take the insulin out), **purification** (remove everything that is not insulin) and **packaging**. It is needed so that a **pure** form of insulin, safe to inject, reaches the patient.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Genetic Engineering"
why: A short lesson on genetic engineering, made for another exam board: read the note beside it before you watch.

title: What other boards add, and what they leave out
md: Clips made for the other boards usually spend time on **GM crops** and name **ligase**, an enzyme that joins the ends. CCEA asks for neither. They often stop before the **fermenter** and **downstreaming**, which CCEA does ask for, so learn those from this lesson.

prompt: The three stages of downstreaming, in order, are extraction, ______ and packaging.
explain: Downstreaming turns the broth into a medicine: first extract the insulin from it, then purify it by removing everything that is not insulin, then package it. The middle stage, the one that makes it safe to inject, is purification.

md: Insulin used to be taken from the pancreases of pigs and cattle: close to human insulin but not the same, and only as much as the abattoirs could supply. Each advantage in the figure answers one of those problems.

**Identical.** Insulin from the modified bacteria is human insulin, made from the human gene.
**Plenty.** Bacteria multiply without limit, so it is made in large quantities.
**Cheaper.** A fermenter costs less than herds of animals.
**No animal.** People with ethical or religious objections to animal products can use it.

prompt: Which of these is an advantage of making insulin with genetically modified bacteria?
options: it is identical to human insulin
it needs no genes at all
it is made without any protein
answer: it is identical to human insulin
explain: The four advantages each answer a problem with animal insulin: it is identical to human insulin, it comes in large quantities, it is cheaper, and no animal is used. The gene and the protein are the whole point of the method, not something it avoids. So the advantage here is that it is identical to human insulin.

md: **One-mark names come first** (every year). Genome, restriction, sticky ends, plasmid, fermenter, downstreaming: each has been a one-mark part. Write the exact name. Describing the ends as loose or matching is not naming them.

**How many processes?** The fermenter question has asked for one, two and four (2022 to 2024). A process is something the bacteria or their plasmids do; warm and fed are conditions, and conditions earn nothing.

A full four-mark answer, one process a line, with the mark each line earns:
1. The bacteria multiply. [1]
2. Their plasmids are copied. [1]
3. The bacteria make their own proteins. [1]
4. They make human insulin. [1]

prompt: A question asks for four processes inside the fermenter. Which of these lines earns nothing?
options: the fermenter is kept warm
the bacteria multiply
the plasmids are copied
explain: A process is something the bacteria or their plasmids do; a condition is what the fermenter provides so that they can do it. Multiplying and copying plasmids are processes the scheme has credited. Kept warm is a condition, so that is the line that earns nothing.

md: **The enzyme is described in the stem** (2019, 2025): its sequence, where it cuts, and that it reads both ways. Mark every site on the top strand, cut each one, then count.
**Hormone, protein, amino acids** (2024). Insulin is a hormone; as a molecule it is a protein, built from amino acids. The bacteria make it because they carry the human gene.

caption: Three sites, three staggered cuts, four sections: the last part of a question that began with base pairing.

md: The hardest shape ends a DNA question with genetic engineering: a base percentage, then the amino acids, then the cuts. The whole chain, worked:

**1. Bases pair.** T pairs with A: if T is 20%, so is A; C and G share the other 60%: C is 30%.
**2. Three bases, one amino acid.** 24 bases code for 24 ÷ 3 = 8 amino acids.
**3. Now the enzyme.** TCGA at bases 3 to 6, 9 to 12 and 18 to 21: 3 staggered cuts, 4 sections.

title: Where the specification stops
md: CCEA names only the restriction enzyme. The enzyme that seals the join, how a gene is read, and real enzyme names are not examined.

prompt: In a length of DNA, 24% of the bases are T. What percentage of the bases are C?
explain: T pairs with A, so A is 24% as well: 48% together. C and G pair with each other, so they share the rest equally: 100 − 48 = 52, and 52 ÷ 2 = 26. So C is 26%.

Explain why the **same enzyme** cuts gene and plasmid; the plasmid carries the **gene**, not the hormone.
Draw the modified bacterium, list the fermenter's processes, give the advantages.

This is a Higher question near the end of B2, seven to ten marks, sometimes the last part of a DNA question. It opens with one-mark names: genome, restriction, sticky ends, downstreaming. The later marks ask you to describe a stage, list the fermenter's processes, or work on a base sequence. Stuck on a describe question?
